mfg1-electrical-l064.title: Identify wire types and connection hardware
mfg1-electrical-l064.objective: Read identifiers and actual specifications, and preserve connection and fastening combinations.

paragraphs.title: Compare identifiers with specifications
paragraphs.text: IV, KIV, and KV identify wires with different structures and uses. Check voltage classification, temperature, solid/stranded construction, conductor area, insulation, and destination against specifications. Do not make textbook color or thickness examples mandatory for every installation.

paragraphs.title: Select tools by purpose
paragraphs.text: Pliers, long-nose pliers, cutters, and strippers differ in holding, bending, cutting, and insulation removal. Match crimp terminals both to the conductor and mounting screw, and check the tool die profile. Distinguish removal of an outer sheath from conductor insulation.

paragraphs.title: Preserve fastening arrangements
paragraphs.text: Nuts, plain washers, spring washers, and captive-washer screws have specified combinations and uses. Trapezoidal threads are used in feed mechanisms and similar applications. If material or fastening target changes, check the drawing; do not omit orientation or quantity on your own judgment.

terms.meaning: An outer covering around a whole cable.
The profile of the tool portion acting on material during crimping or similar work.
A thread with a trapezoidal profile, used for feed mechanisms and similar applications.
An identifier for vinyl-insulated wire for electrical equipment.

mfg1-electrical-l064.activity:
30-minute study target: reading 10 minutes, organizing examples 8, writing 9, reflection 3.
Make a four-way checklist for wire, terminal, tool, and mounting screw. Explain mm versus mm²and the sheath versus individual conductor insulation.
safety: Do not test unknown wire or terminal suitability by energizing it.
mfg1-electrical-l064.summary: Read identifiers and actual specifications, and preserve connection and fastening combinations.

mfg1-electrical-l065.title: Solder materials, flux, and rework
mfg1-electrical-l065.objective: Combine material, surface condition, heat, restraint, and inspection.

paragraphs.title: Alloys and conditions
paragraphs.text: Leaded and lead-free solders differ in composition, melting point, wetting, and other properties. For example, Sn 63/Pb 37 and Sn-Ag-Cu systems discussed in the textbook may require different conditions. Do not claim every lead-free joint is inferior; use the qualified materials and process conditions for the product.

paragraphs.title: Preparing the surface
paragraphs.text: Flux helps act on oxides and supports wetting. Combine cleaning, suitable heating, restraint, supply, cooling, and inspection. Residue cleaning requirements and solvents depend on flux and specifications; do not wash every product in one liquid.

paragraphs.title: Correct without creating more defects
paragraphs.text: Match tip shape and condition to the component, avoiding lifted lands from prolonged heating or force. Identify bridges, cracks, and insufficient solder, and use approved rework and reinspection. Shine alone does not determine connection quality.

terms.meaning: A material helping oxide treatment and wetting during soldering.
Material left after a process.
A conductive board area used to connect component terminals and similar parts.
A fracture in material or a joint.

mfg1-electrical-l065.activity:
30-minute study target: reading 10 minutes, organizing examples 8, writing 9, reflection 3.
Make checks for material labels, process conditions, residue treatment, inspection, and rework approval. Report a suspected mixture of different alloys.
safety: Check product information and procedures for lead and cleaning agents, ventilation, and burn prevention.
mfg1-electrical-l065.summary: Combine material, surface condition, heat, restraint, and inspection.

mfg1-electrical-l066.title: Passive components and devices using temperature or vibration
mfg1-electrical-l066.objective: Check structure, characteristics, ratings, and purpose as well as nominal value.

paragraphs.title: Resistors also have types
paragraphs.text: Carbon-film, metal-based, wirewound, chip, variable, and preset resistors differ in structure and use. Even at the same resistance, compare power, temperature coefficient, dimensions, and frequency behavior. Confirm variable-resistor terminals and adjustment range too.

paragraphs.title: Distinguish what is stored
paragraphs.text: Capacitors and coils are passive components storing energy associated with electric and magnetic fields respectively. Read specified capacitance, inductance, and permissible current. “Passive” does not mean safe to touch: residual charge and heat still require care.

paragraphs.title: Use special characteristics
paragraphs.text: Thermistors use resistance changes with temperature; piezoelectric devices use the relation between force and electricity; quartz resonators use stable vibration properties. Distinguish them from light receivers and emitters; do not swap lookalike parts without authorization.

terms.meaning: Components that consume, store, or release energy supplied externally.
A device using resistance changes with temperature.
A device using the relationship between force and electricity.

terms.reading: すいしょうしんどうし
terms.meaning: A component using quartz vibration properties.

mfg1-electrical-l066.activity:
30-minute study target: reading 10 minutes, organizing examples 8, writing 9, reflection 3.
Summarize functions and specification checks for resistors, capacitors, coils, thermistors, and quartz devices. State two hazards remaining even with passive components.
safety: Do not omit power isolation and residual-energy checks for passive components.
mfg1-electrical-l066.summary: Check structure, characteristics, ratings, and purpose as well as nominal value.

mfg1-electrical-l067.title: Distinguish lathes, milling machines, and NC machines
mfg1-electrical-l067.objective: Distinguish machines by what rotates and what they machine.

paragraphs.title: Identify what rotates
paragraphs.text: A lathe rotates the workpiece while a cutting tool machines outside and inside diameters, grooves, or threads. A milling machine rotates the cutter and uses relative motion against a secured workpiece to machine planes, sides, steps, and grooves. Product shape alone does not uniquely identify the machine.

paragraphs.title: Drilling and grinding
paragraphs.text: A drill press secures the workpiece and machines holes with drills, reamers, or similar tools. A grinder gradually removes material with a grinding wheel. Drills, lathe tools, and end mills differ in cutting-edge location and machine use; do not substitute lookalike tools.

paragraphs.title: Numerical control and automatic changes
paragraphs.text: NC is the general term for numerical control, including NC lathes, NC mills, and machining centers. A machining center has automatic tool changing. A program does not remove the need to check datum, tool, fixture, and interference; unattended operation is not unconditionally safe.

terms.meaning: A cutting tool used on lathes or similar machines.
Numerical control.
An NC machine tool with automatic tool changing.
Unintended contact between tools, parts, or similar objects.

mfg1-electrical-l067.activity:
30-minute study target: reading 10 minutes, organizing examples 8, writing 9, reflection 3.
For shaft outside diameter, a flat groove, many holes, and ground finishing, select the machine and identify what rotates. Describe checks before the first machining operation.
safety: Do not touch chucks, wheels, or rotating tools. Follow stopping, isolation, and assigned procedures.
mfg1-electrical-l067.summary: Distinguish machines by what rotates and what they machine.

mfg1-electrical-l068.title: Calculate resistance from dimensions, power, and energy
mfg1-electrical-l068.objective: Align material, dimensions, and fixed conditions; distinguish W from Wh.

paragraphs.title: Wire length and area
paragraphs.text: For the same material and temperature, R=ρℓ/S: resistance increases with length and decreases with cross-sectional area. Ifρ is inΩ·m and length in m, area must be in m². Do not substitute diameter as area; retain material and temperature conditions.

paragraphs.title: Rate of consumption and total amount
paragraphs.text: For a DC resistor, P=VI=I²R=V²/R gives power in W. Energy is power multiplied by time, in Wh or similar units. At 12 V and 60 Ω, I=0.2 A and P=2.4 W; over 30 minutes this is 1.2 Wh. W and Wh are different quantities.

paragraphs.title: Calculation versus component selection
paragraphs.text: At constant voltage, a smaller resistance gives greater power; at constant current, a larger resistance gives greater power. State what is held constant. Do not select equipment from calculated power alone: check rated power, cooling, temperature, and protection.

terms.meaning: A quantity describing a material’s resistance to current flow.
The area of a cut section.
Energy per unit time.
Total electrical energy over a given time.

mfg1-electrical-l068.activity:
30-minute study target: reading 10 minutes, organizing examples 8, writing 9, reflection 3.
Find the resistance ratio for the same material at twice the length and three times the area. For 24 V and 120 Ω, calculate current, power, and energy over 15 minutes with units.
safety: Do not use calculated values to justify unauthorized connections or exceeding ratings.
mfg1-electrical-l068.summary: Align material, dimensions, and fixed conditions; distinguish W from Wh.

mfg1-electrical-l069.title: AC period and phase, and DC transients
mfg1-electrical-l069.objective: Read frequency as complete cycles, and distinguish ideal steady state from actual transients.

paragraphs.title: A complete repetition is one cycle
paragraphs.text: Sine-wave frequency counts complete repetitions per second, not simply direction reversals. One cycle is 20 ms at 50 Hz and about 16.7 ms at 60 Hz. Check nameplate frequency, not location alone.

paragraphs.title: Time differences between voltage and current
paragraphs.text: In an ideal purely resistive sine-wave circuit, voltage and current are in phase. Current lags voltage for an ideal coil and leads it for an ideal capacitor. Compare equivalent phase points; do not confuse different waveform heights with time displacement. Actual circuits include losses and multiple components.

paragraphs.title: DC also has transitional behavior
paragraphs.text: Do not apply an ideal coil or capacitor’s DC steady-state description unchanged immediately after connection or interruption. These components are also used in real DC circuits. Consider capacitor charging and residual charge, and voltage associated with changing coil current; do not short components yourself.

terms.meaning: A position within a periodic change.
Corresponding periodic changes occurring with the same timing.
The transition toward steady state after conditions change.

terms.reading: ていじょうじょうたい
terms.meaning: A state in which changes have settled.

mfg1-electrical-l069.activity:
30-minute study target: reading 10 minutes, organizing examples 8, writing 9, reflection 3.
Find a 25 Hz period in ms. Explain voltage/current relationships for ideal R, L, and C, and why DC steady-state descriptions alone cannot establish safety.
safety: Do not experiment on real equipment by switching supplies or shorting energy-storage components.
mfg1-electrical-l069.summary: Read frequency as complete cycles, and distinguish ideal steady state from actual transients.

mfg1-electrical-l070.title: Check series-parallel calculations with Kirchhoff’s laws
mfg1-electrical-l070.objective: Set directions and polarities, then check balances after combining circuit portions.

paragraphs.title: Balance at a node
paragraphs.text: Kirchhoff’s current law equates total incoming and outgoing current at a node. If 8 mA enters and splits into 3 mA and another branch, the other branch is 5 mA. Keep assumed directions consistent; a negative result indicates the opposite direction.

paragraphs.title: Add signed potential differences around a loop
paragraphs.text: The voltage law makes the sum of signed potential differences around a loop zero. A12 V rise and drops of 4 V and 8 V give 12−4−8=0. Do not add all voltages as positive: establish traversal direction and polarity.

paragraphs.title: Combine portions in sequence
paragraphs.text: Series components carry the same current; parallel components share terminal voltage. For example,120 Ωparallel to 240 Ωgives 80 Ω; adding 40 Ωin series gives 120 Ω. Find total current, section voltages, and branch currents, then check both laws.

terms.meaning: A point connecting circuit branches.
A circuit path returning to its starting point.
The law that balances current entering and leaving a node.
The law that signed potential differences sum to zero around a loop.

mfg1-electrical-l070.activity:
30-minute study target: reading 10 minutes, organizing examples 8, writing 9, reflection 3.
For an ideal 18 V source with 40 Ωin series with 120 Ωparallel to 240 Ω, calculate total current, parallel-section voltage, and both branch currents, and verify the balances.
safety: Do not treat an ideal teaching circuit as wiring instructions for real equipment.
mfg1-electrical-l070.summary: Set directions and polarities, then check balances after combining circuit portions.
